meta.question: Why does AI sometimes make things up?

facts.claim: Language models generate text by predicting likely next words rather than looking facts up, and have no built-in fact-checking
Pretraining shows a model only examples of fluent language, with no true/false labels, so fluent output can be wrong
Arbitrary low-frequency facts, like a birthday, cannot be predicted from patterns alone and lead to hallucinations
Accuracy-only tests give zero for a blank answer, so guessing scores better than saying I don't know, and models learn to guess
Researchers propose penalizing confident errors more than expressions of uncertainty
In 2023 lawyers filed a court brief citing fake cases produced by ChatGPT; the judge found them fictitious and fined the lawyers and firm $5,000
Checking AI output remains essential, and giving the model a reference source to work from can help

post.yt_caption: Why does AI make things up? Imagine your AI recommends a book with an author and a page number, and it does not exist. Next-word prediction, facts that cannot be guessed from patterns, and tests that reward guessing, explained step by step. Follow FredsDesk for daily AI
post.pinned_comment: The person in this story is fictional and the story is an illustration. The facts come from OpenAI research and news reports: models predict likely words rather than look facts up, arbitrary facts cannot be predicted from patterns alone, and tests that score only accuracy reward guessing. The 2023 New York court case is real. The two tips at the end are practical suggestions, not guarantees.
